A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched across additions, relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on Kubric, LIBERO and Physics101, alongside ablations, qualitative evaluations and a user study.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Cityscapes evaluation, multi-frame conditioning, joint video/trajectory generation and sampling-density experiments.

M1.justification: The original trajectory VAE and flow-matching core remains. However, v2 adds trained multi-frame conditioning with temporal embeddings and variable context (Appendix A.2), plus joint RGB/trajectory generation through concatenated latent channels (Section 4.3). These substantially extend the model's inputs and outputs.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cityscapes urban driving, including camera turns, traffic and pedestrians, beyond the earlier controlled physical and robotics scenes. It also evaluates forecasting with two conditioning frames on Kubric, changing the information available about initial motion. Earlier coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds the SD3.5 + Tracks joint-generation configuration to the existing RGB-only and trajectory-only comparison. External baseline membership in retained experiments is unchanged; the new Cityscapes evaluation uses the already evaluated Track2Act and WAN.

E3.justification: New protocols include approximately 3,000 training and 500 validation Cityscapes clips from separate locations, with 28×56 trajectory grids; matched one-frame/two-frame Kubric evaluations; and density comparisons on a common 8×8 subgrid. The density study reports best scores across checkpoints at epochs 350, 375 and 400. Existing protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 directly tests whether denser grids improve forecasting (Table 17), additional input frames reduce ambiguity (Table 12 and Figures 4–5), and joint trajectory generation improves motion in generated RGB video (Table 6). These add substantial controlled analyses while retaining the earlier ablations and robustness tests.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit sampling information for new evaluations: eight differently seeded predictions per Cityscapes clip and three predictions per multi-frame input configuration. These are generation samples, not repeated training runs. Existing standard-deviation reporting is retained, without new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing scores are retained, while substantial new results appear. Cityscapes mean MSE is 1565.06 for the proposed model, 3495.43 for WAN and 9305.63 for Track2Act (Table 9). Joint generation achieves in-distribution LRTL 28.2 versus 33.7 for RGB-only SD3.5 (Table 6). Tables 12 and 17 add context-length and density findings under new experimental conditions.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 extends the formal target from p(X|I) to a family of distributions conditioned on a variable number of images. The original VAE and flow objectives, rigidity metric and variance definition are unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, numbered introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims about stochastic dense trajectory forecasting, advantages over prior predictors, and the overhead of RGB generation. The added experiments do not revise these statements.

C2.justification: v2 explains how observing velocity reduces predictive diversity while occlusions preserve ambiguity, discusses conditioning-related failures on Cityscapes, and interprets joint generation as improving RGB motion rigidity. The earlier mechanism explanations and limitations section remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies targeted implementation details for the additions: Cityscapes preprocessing and CoTracker3 labeling, joint VAE resolution and latent channels, multi-frame temporal embeddings, and density-study training and checkpoint rules. The existing architecture, hyperparameter and hardware tables remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Walker et al. (2016), Li et al. (2018) and AllTracker, explaining distinctions in trajectory compression, temporal consistency, VAE usage and evaluation. This improves positioning against relevant earlier approaches without substantially reorganizing the existing literature discussion.

P1.justification: v2 expands selected experimental and related-work passages, subdivides real-world evaluation and adds appendix subsections. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain intact. Publication headers and author formatting change, and the acknowledgements are removed.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual evidence with multi-frame comparisons, additional Physics101 examples, Cityscapes panels and new evaluation tables, while extending Table 6. The original Physics101 Figure 4 is retained as appendix Figure 8. Existing visual material is preserved despite relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a direct density control and confined quantitative real-world evaluation to controlled Physics101 scenes. v2 adds a common-subgrid density experiment (Table 17) and urban driving evaluation across held-out locations (Table 9), substantially strengthening support for dense scene modeling and its applicability. Multi-frame and joint-generation experiments provide further targeted evidence. These gains materially improve the paper despite continued limited statistical uncertainty reporting.
